> The "Professor Jiang" (full name Jiang Xueqin) operation has all the hallmarks of a low-effort grift that happens to align neatly with Beijing's interests.  
>   
> 1. The "Professor" title is straight-up fraudulent marketing  
>   
> He repeatedly introduced himself on camera and in videos as "Professor Jiang," "your professor for today," "welcome to my class," etc. Then, when confronted (as in the viral clips), he denies ever saying it and blames "the internet." Wikipedia and every neutral source confirms: BA in English literature from Yale (1999), high school/private academy teacher in Beijing, education reform guy. No university post, no grad degree in history/politics, no publications in the field. It's pure YouTube theater, class room, slides, lecturing tone, to trigger "expert" vibes.  
>   
> 2. His "expertise" is nonexistent  
>   
> The guy teaches high school in Beijing. His channel (Predictive History) slaps on Asimov's fictional "psychohistory," game theory buzzwords, and "structural analysis" for bold geopolitical takes. One of his lectures flat-out claims Hannibal Barca (and the Battle of Cannae) was basically Roman propaganda fiction/myth-making. That's not edgy revisionism, that's crank pseudohistory. Hannibal is one of the best-documented figures in antiquity (Polybius, Livy, coins, archaeology, multiple independent sources). Real historians don't touch this. It was the exact moment I (and plenty of others) clocked him as unserious. He rode virality from a few "accurate" predictions (Trump 2024 win + US-Iran escalation, which played out in 2025-26) into TV spots. Media books the aesthetic and clicks, not the CV.  
>   
> 3. The China angle and "asset" question  
>   
> He's Chinese-Canadian (born China 1976, moved to Canada young, back to Beijing now). Early 2000s: mildly dissident, filmed worker protests for PBS, got detained/expelled by CCP security. Then magically allowed back, built a career in Chinese education reform, and now runs English-language geopolitics content from inside China (where YouTube is blocked for normal people). He has ties to China Youth Daily (formerly wrote for it, an official CCP youth league paper). Lives and teaches freely in Beijing while pumping content that reaches millions in the West.  
>   
> His output:  
>   
> Predicts/frames US decline, overreach, hubris, and inevitable multipolar world.  
> US should "dialogue" with China/Russia/Iran instead of confronting.  
> China is inward-focused, self-sufficient "Middle Kingdom," not a threat seeking hegemony.  
> Codependency with US; conflict overblown.  
>   
> This is textbook soft-power alignment. China's geopolitical sweet spot right now?   
>   
> US isolationism under Trump-style "America First." It fractures alliances (Europe, Indo-Pacific), diverts US resources inward, weakens coordinated containment (AUKUS, QUAD, NATO), and gives Beijing breathing room on Taiwan, South China Sea, tech decoupling, etc. Chinese analysts have openly preferred unpredictable bilateral Trump deals over Biden-era multilateral pressure. Jiang's narrative doesn't always scream "vote Trump" but it does scream "US is doomed anyway, don't fight it, just accept multipolarity." That's catnip for demoralizing Western audiences while Beijing plays the long game.

Gordon Chang and others call him CCP-run for a reason; operating that freely from Beijing while hitting every pro-multipolar note isn't coincidence. Repetitious Hypnosis

Purpose: The primary goal is to change deeply ingrained behaviors or negative patterns by turning positive suggestions into "habits of the mind".

Techniques: Hypnotists may use the same phrase repeatedly or rephrase the same message in different ways throughout a session to increase effectiveness.

Subconscious Relearning: Similar to learning a new skill, repetition allows the subconscious to accept new information, making it useful for treating anxiety or breaking habits.

"Rule of Three": A common hypnotic rule where a core suggestion is stated at least three times to maximize the effect, often woven into metaphors or rapport building.

Effect on Brain: Repetition helps narrow attention, reduces critical thinking from the conscious mind, and helps the brain become comfortable with new, positive patterns.

Factcheck with AI - feel free to check
(0:44) "America may START bombing energy infrastructure" — ❌ Wrong. This was happening from day one of Operation Epic Fury.
(2:23) Ground invasion "as early as this weekend" — ❌ Wrong. Still unauthorized as of April 2.
(6:06) ~50,000 US troops in the Middle East — ✅ Correct. Confirmed by Pentagon briefings.
(6:22) Letter to reserves telling them to prepare to deploy — ✅ Correct. Confirmed in multiple reports.
(9:17) America would lose a ground war in Iran — ⚠ Opinion presented as fact. Widely shared view among analysts but not settled.
(9:33) Losing would collapse the petrodollar and American empire — ⚠ Speculative theory presented as inevitable outcome.
(11:10) Japan gets 75% of its oil from the Middle East — ✅ Roughly correct.
(11:48) JP Morgan says world runs out of oil by mid-April — ❌ Exaggerated. JP Morgan warned Gulf oil deliveries halt by mid-April, not that the world runs out — and the US was unlikely to face physical shortages, just higher prices. Newsweek
(14:51) "America took over Venezuela" — ✅ Largely accurate. US special forces seized Maduro and the US announced indefinite control over Venezuelan oil sales. Council on Foreign Relations
(21:17) War knocks out all GCC oil production — ⚠ Oversimplified. The Strait blockade disrupts delivery, not production itself. Saudi Arabia's output hasn't been destroyed.
(22:48) America is $39 trillion in debt — ✅ Correct at time of recording.
(25:24) Putin proved the strategy works in Ukraine — ⚠ Contested. Russia's economy is under severe strain; whether Ukraine proves the strategy "works" is highly debatable.
(29:35) "Dugan, 1996 book" — ❌ Wrong on both. It's Alexander Dugin, published 1997.
(33:24) Russia controlling Ukraine gives it one-third of world's carbohydrates — ⚠ Exaggerated. Ukraine is a major grain exporter but "one-third of world's carbohydrates" overstates it significantly.
(39:43) Trump's agenda is driven by "love of the white race" — ⚠ Editorializing. Christian nationalism is a real framework some use to describe MAGA, but "love of the white race" is the presenter's characterization, not established fact.

The water map starting at around 17:30 is heavily misleading. The map displays absolute values of total renewable water resources, puts these values in a "good/bad" metric and is taken from wikipedia. The problem with that depiction is that large countries are most certainly performing better than small countries. Thats like comparing total GDP to measure individual wealth in a country. The US performs very well in that graphic compared to Europe, because Europe has been split into different countries and the US not. 

Summing up the values for each individual EU country gives a similar amount of water as the US has, so no dependency in that regard.

This is all pretty superficial… 

A couple points:
Venezuela is not in North America… I don’t know what else to say.

Nitrogen is not the only fertilizer - and of the many fertilizers, many countries have the capability of producing more themselves, they haven’t because global trade reduces that necessity. Given a change in supply chain reliability, countries will adapt and increase production in strategic regions. Urea for example is imported by Brazil, yet Brazil could in a matter of 3-5 years produce all its urea at home.

Lastly these resources are not just easily accessible, they require some time to build infrastructure and ramp up production. Even Canada and America don’t have enough refining capacity to simply just flip a switch and replace the ME in supplying oil to the world. It would take 5+ years to achieve those levels. In the meantime other countries would also be exploring these options. Brazil for instance again, produces more than enough crude oil for its population (especially given ethanol production and flex motors) - but has a gap in diesel production which it has been targeting to close by 2030 - by building refineries.

Water, again - desalinization is used in many countries. Requires energy. Industry - requires energy. Europe could move towards this, they don’t because they have foolishly prioritized environmental cultism over practicality and “perfection” over “good enough”. Europe could feasibly reopen coal plants and bring energy prices down.

So this analysis is flawed in that it takes a snapshot and assumes actors in the game don’t make moves to amend their existing gaps.

### **@morty-et3jf**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xrmERlHUqBk&lc=Ugwocm0k1BXJSTtk3rR4AaABAg)

The idea of a “New World Order” (NWO) conspiracy sounds dramatic—but most versions of it collapse pretty quickly when you look at how power actually works in the real world.
Let’s break it down honestly.
What people mean by “New World Order”
Typically, NWO theories claim that:
A small secret group (elites, billionaires, governments, etc.) is planning to control the entire world
They want a single global government
Events like wars, pandemics, or economic crises are planned to push that agenda
Common groups mentioned:
United Nations
World Economic Forum
Illuminati
Central banks / global financial institutions
The reality check (this is where most people don’t think deeply)
1. Coordination problem
You’re assuming thousands of powerful people across countries:
Never leak anything meaningful
Never betray each other
Stay perfectly aligned for decades
That’s not how humans behave. Even small companies can’t keep secrets—forget global domination plans.
2. Governments don’t even cooperate well now
Look at:
Trade wars
Border conflicts
Political rivalries
If countries can’t agree on climate policy, how are they secretly agreeing to run a single world system?
3. Real power is messy, not unified
Power is:
Competing interests
Corporations vs governments
Countries vs countries
Internal political fights
There’s influence, yes—but not one master control room.
Why the theory spreads anyway
Here’s the uncomfortable truth:
1. Humans hate uncertainty
It’s psychologically easier to believe:
“Someone is in control”
than:
“The world is chaotic and no one fully controls it”
2. Pattern-seeking brain
Your brain is wired to connect dots—even when they’re unrelated:
Same people attend conferences → “They’re planning something”
Global events happen → “It must be coordinated”
3. Real distrust (this part is valid)
Institutions do have:
Corruption
Hidden agendas
Lobbying influence
That’s where conspiracy theories get traction—there’s a grain of truth, but it gets exaggerated into fantasy.
The more grounded version (what’s actually happening)
Instead of a secret NWO, what you actually have is:
Powerful organizations trying to influence global policy
Wealthy individuals shaping markets and politics
Governments cooperating when it benefits them
That’s not a conspiracy—it’s just power dynamics.
Brutally honest conclusion
There is no unified “New World Order” controlling everything.
But:
There are powerful groups trying to gain more influence
There is inequality in who holds power
There is manipulation—but it’s fragmented, not centralized
